title: Γεωργός καὶ παῖδες αὐτοῦ
part: The Farmer and his Sons (Chambry 83 · Perry 42)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 83 (= Perry 42). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γεωργός τις μέλλων καταλύειν τὸν βίον καὶ βουλόμενος τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ παῖδας πεῖραν λαβεῖν τῆς γεωργίας, προσκαλεσάμενος αὐτοὺς ἔφη· « Παῖδες ἐμοί, ἐγὼ μὲν ἤδη τοῦ βίου ὑπέξειμι, ὑμεῖς δ᾽ ἅπερ ἐν τῇ ἀμπέλῳ μοι κέκρυπται ζητήσαντες, εὑρήσετε πάντα. »
sentences.tr: Geōrgos tis mellōn katalyein ton bion kai boulomenos tous heautou paidas peiran labein tēs geōrgias, proskalesamenos autous ephē· « Paides emoi, egō men ēdē tou biou hypexeimi, hymeis d’ haper en tēi ampelōi moi kekryptai zētēsantes, heurēsete panta. »
sentences.l: A certain farmer, being about to end his life and wishing his own sons to make trial of farming, having called them to him, said: « My sons, I am already departing out of life; but you, once you have sought for the things that have been hidden by me in the vineyard, will find them all. »
sentences.i: A certain farmer, on the point of ending his life and wanting his sons to gain experience of farming, called them to him and said: « My sons, I am already on my way out of life; but search for what I have hidden in the vineyard, and you will find it all. »
sentences.n: Two settled phrases for dying stand side by side: καταλύειν τὸν βίον, 'to break up one's life' as one breaks camp, and ὑπέξειμι, 'go out from under'. πεῖραν λαβεῖν takes the genitive of the thing tried. ἅπερ … κέκρυπται is a neuter plural subject with a singular verb, which is the Greek rule, not a slip; μοι κέκρυπται is a perfect passive with the dative of agent — the regular construction with this tense: 'has been hidden by me'. ἄμπελος is strictly the vine, but here, with a whole ground to dig, it stands for the planting as a whole. Note what the father does not say: he never uses the word treasure.

sentences.t: Οἱ μὲν οὖν οἰηθέντες θησαυρὸν ἐκεῖ που κατορωρύχθαι, πᾶσαν τὴν τῆς ἀμπέλου γῆν μετὰ τὴν ἀποβίωσιν τοῦ πατρὸς κατέσκαψαν.
sentences.tr: Hoi men oun oiēthentes thēsauron ekei pou katorōrychthai, pasan tēn tēs ampelou gēn meta tēn apobiōsin tou patros kateskapsan.
sentences.l: They then, supposing that a treasure had been buried somewhere there, dug over all the ground of the vineyard after their father's death.
sentences.n: οἰηθέντες is passive in form and active in sense, from οἴομαι, 'suppose'; what they supposed is reported by the infinitive κατορωρύχθαι, the perfect passive of κατορύσσω. The enclitic που, 'somewhere', is where the guessing shows.

sentences.t: Καὶ θησαυρῷ μὲν οὐ περιέτυχον, ἡ δὲ ἄμπελος καλῶς σκαφεῖσα πολλαπλασίονα τὸν καρπὸν ἀνέδωκεν.
sentences.tr: Kai thēsaurōi men ou perietychon, hē de ampelos kalōs skapheisa pollaplasiona ton karpon anedōken.
sentences.l: And upon a treasure they did not come, but the vineyard, well dug over, gave up many times the fruit.
sentences.i: They came upon no treasure, but the vineyard, thoroughly dug over, yielded many times the crop.
sentences.n: περιτυγχάνω takes the dative of what one falls in with. σκαφεῖσα is the aorist passive of σκάπτω — the same digging as the κατέσκαψαν that closed the sentence before: the labour they spent on one thing quietly did the other.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ὁ κάματος θησαυρός ἐστι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ho kamatos thēsauros esti tois anthrōpois.
sentences.l: The fable shows that toil is a treasure for men.
sentences.n: κάματος is the hard work and the weariness it costs, in one word. The dative τοῖς ἀνθρώποις names those for whom it is a treasure.
